citation: Dede, C. (2009). Comparing Frameworks for "21st Century Skills". Harvard Graduate School of Education. https://eric.ed.gov
title: Partnership for 21st Century Skills (P21) framework
description: The P21 framework (2006) serves as the chapter's baseline because it is "more detailed and more widely adopted than any of the alternatives". It comprises core subjects, 21st century content (global awareness, financial and civic literacy, health awareness), learning and thinking skills (critical thinking, communication, creativity, collaboration, contextual learning, information and media literacy), ICT literacy, and life skills such as leadership, ethics, and adaptability. P21 also advocates authentic assessments integrated with core subject assessments.
requirements: Assessments must measure all five results that matter, with 21st century skills assessment integrated with core subjects
constraints: Standardized tests alone can measure only a few of the important skills and knowledge students should learn
target_learning_goals: Core subjects plus 21st century content, thinking skills, ICT literacy, and life skills
examples: The chapter outlines P21's five result areas and its position that separate assessments of 21st century skills would defeat infusion into core subjects
key_sources: Dede, C. (2009). Comparing Frameworks for "21st Century Skills". Harvard Graduate School of Education. https://eric.ed.gov

article_title: Teachers’ AI digital competencies and twenty-first century skills in the post-pandemic world
citation: Davy Tsz Kit Ng, Jac Ka Lok Leung, Jiahong Su, Ross Chi Wui Ng, Samuel Kai Wah Chu. (2023). Teachers' AI digital competencies and twenty-first century skills in the post-pandemic world. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10203-6
title: P21's framework for twenty-first century learning adapted for AI-era teacher competencies
description: The article applies P21's framework for twenty-first century learning to identify four key teacher competencies for online teaching with AI: core subjects, 3Rs and twenty-first century themes; learning and innovation skills; information, media and technology skills; and life and career skills. It emphasizes that teacher competencies "should not only focus on acquisition of basic AI knowledge and skills, but also cultivation of the qualities necessary for the teacher's adaptation to, survival in and control over future society". Examples span AI writing assistants, book recommendation systems, and workplace AI capability sets.
requirements: Universities could educate the teacher workforce to integrate AI applications throughout students' lifecycle
constraints: The paper does not focus on technological/computer science knowledge but on broader digital competencies
examples: Cetindamar et al. (2022) highlighted four sets of workplace capabilities associated with AI, including technological skills and human-machine interaction
key_sources: Davy Tsz Kit Ng, Jac Ka Lok Leung, Jiahong Su, Ross Chi Wui Ng, Samuel Kai Wah Chu. (2023). Teachers' AI digital competencies and twenty-first century skills in the post-pandemic world. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10203-6

article_title: Towards a standardized competency-profile for peer-to-peer-teachers in medical education - a systematic mapping review.
citation: Bernhard-Skala Christian, Steinweg Bernhard. (2026). Towards a standardized competency-profile for peer-to-peer-teachers in medical education - a systematic mapping review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09997-9
title: Draft competency-profile for qualifying student P2P-teachers in human medicine
description: A qualitative competency-profile aggregating the competencies found across 18 studies, organized into medical contents (medical knowledge and skills, technical equipment, interprofessional content such as ISBAR), educational and training knowledge and skills (application of learning theories, course planning, organizational coordination, teaching methodologies, presentations, learning environment, small-group leadership, time management, assessment and feedback), professional development (evaluation and self-reflection), and organizational competencies. The draft "reflects the interplay of medical skills, on the one hand (yellow colors), and teaching skills (blue colors), on the other hand", treating them as two sides of the same coin without ranking them.
requirements: Requires profound reflection of definitions and of learning goals beyond naming categories and anchors
constraints: The figure does not represent quantities or training priorities; the profile is far from complete and serves as a starting point for discussion, not a curriculum
target_learners: student P2P-teachers (student tutors) in human medicine
target_learning_goals: teaching competencies for qualifying student peer teachers across medical subjects
examples: Table 2 lists anchors such as Peyton's four steps, Pendleton's and the Van de Ridder feedback models, and the organization of a large-scale educational event exceeding 1000 participants
key_sources: Bernhard-Skala Christian, Steinweg Bernhard. (2026). Towards a standardized competency-profile for peer-to-peer-teachers in medical education - a systematic mapping review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09997-9

article_title: Integrating 21st Century Skills into Teaching English: Investigating Its Effect on Listening and Speaking Skills
citation: Hamid Ashraf, Fatemeh Ahmadi, Mansooreh Hosseinnia. (2017). Integrating 21st Century Skills into Teaching English: Investigating its Effect on Listening and Speaking Skills. i-manager's Journal on English Language Teaching, Vol. 7 No. 4. https://www.imanagerpublications.com
title: Partnership for 21st Century Skills (P21) framework of learning and innovation, information/media/technology, and life and career skills
description: The article organizes 21st century skills using the Partnership for 21st Century Learning framework, in which skills fall into three categories: "learning and innovation skills", "information, media, and technology skills", and "life and career skills" (Farisi, 2016; Pearson, 2013). The framework rests on "a solid foundation of content knowledge" supported by specific skills, expertise and literacies, and holds that every student should be a critical thinker, problem solver, innovator, effective communicator, self-directed learner, and information- and media-literate. Figure 1 depicts "pools" of standards and assessments, curriculum and instruction, professional development, and learning environment beneath the framework.
requirements: Instructional organization that expands the three skill categories into curriculum, standards and assessment, professional development, and learning environment
examples: The study operationalized the framework as critical thinking and problem solving, communication and collaboration, interpersonal skills, leadership, and technology literacy in EFL lessons
key_sources: Hamid Ashraf, Fatemeh Ahmadi, Mansooreh Hosseinnia. (2017). Integrating 21st Century Skills into Teaching English: Investigating its Effect on Listening and Speaking Skills. i-manager's Journal on English Language Teaching, Vol. 7 No. 4. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1173769

article_title: Influence Based Learning Program Scientific Learning Approach to Science Students Generic Skills
citation: Ida Wahyuni, Khairul Amdani. (2016). Influence Based Learning Program Scientific Learning Approach to Science Students Generic Skills. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.7, No.32. https://www.iiste.org
title: P2BPS: a scientific-approach-based learning program structured as a sequence of scientific-method stages
description: P2BPS is a learning program designed so that students "construct and find their own knowledge through a series of scientific methods". It proceeds through the stages of observing, formulating problems and hypotheses, collecting data by experiment, processing and associating data, drawing conclusions, and communicating what was found. The article applies it in general physics II for prospective physics teachers, beginning each activity with an authentic real problem encountered in everyday life and organizing group investigation, analysis and communication of results to other students.
requirements: Learning activities begin with an authentic real problem found, seen and experienced by students in everyday life
Experiments must give students the opportunity to identify problems, formulate questions and hypotheses, plan and conduct experiments, analyze results, and report and communicate
constraints: Studied in a general physics II course for prospective physics teachers at one Indonesian university; the article does not claim generalization beyond this setting
target_learners: prospective physics teachers (undergraduate physics and mathematics education students)
target_learning_goals: generic science skills such as observation, symbolic language, logical inference, and mathematical modeling
examples: In the study, one class was taught general physics II with P2BPS while a parallel class received conventional lecturer-led learning, and generic science skills were tested before and after
key_sources: Ida Wahyuni, Khairul Amdani. (2016). Influence Based Learning Program Scientific Learning Approach to Science Students Generic Skills. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.7, No.32. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1122435

article_title: Influence Based Learning Program Scientific Learning Approach to Science Students Generic Skills
citation: Ida Wahyuni, Khairul Amdani. (2016). Influence Based Learning Program Scientific Learning Approach to Science Students Generic Skills. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.7, No.32. https://www.iiste.org
title: P2BPS lesson pattern: authentic problem, group investigation, and communication of findings
description: The P2BPS lesson pattern opens with an authentic real problem from students' everyday lives, moves through group investigation in which students observe, question, hypothesize, experiment, and process data, and closes with students communicating findings to peers. The article states that "Learning activities begin with the filing of an authentic real problem is found, seen and experienced by stud ents in everyday life" and that problems are "solved by the investigation group, analyzed and communicated to other students". Experimentation is described as the spirit of the program, serving both experience-based understanding and investigative problem solving.
requirements: An authentic real problem drawn from students' everyday experience as the opening activity
Group investigation with experimentation, including planning, designing, and carrying out experiments and processing data
A communication phase in which results are presented to other students
constraints: Described and tested in university general physics II; the article does not report the pattern in other domains
examples: The experimental class in the study learned general physics II through this pattern while the control class received conventional cooperative-assignment lecturing
key_sources: Ida Wahyuni, Khairul Amdani. (2016). Influence Based Learning Program Scientific Learning Approach to Science Students Generic Skills. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.7, No.32. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1122435
